verdicts.why: The closest finding is F01 ('Unvalidated UTF-8 string decoding from untrusted wire data'), which is the only finding that touches a length field read from the wire: 'The byte array length is read as a single unsigned byte (line 68), limiting maximum short-string length to 255 bytes.' But F01 is about charset validity — malformed UTF-8 producing replacement characters and semantic/data-corruption effects — not about an attacker-controlled length driving an allocation made before the payload is known to be present. It mentions the length read only in passing, and to argue the length is bounded (255), which is the opposite of the pre-allocation exhaustion mechanism D1 describes. F02 is about recursion depth, not allocation sizing. No finding claims that a declared length causes a buffer to be created ahead of verifying the corresponding bytes exist.

verdicts.quote: The readFieldValue() method (line 158-221) is recursive. It calls readTable() at line 181 for case 'F', and readArray() at line 184 for case 'A'. The readTable() method (lines 139-155) calls readFieldValue() again (line 150). The readArray() method (lines 237-249) also calls readFieldValue() again (line 245). There is no recursion depth limit checked in any of these methods.
verdicts.why: F02 describes exactly D2's mechanism: the decoding routines readFieldValue/readTable/readArray call one another in a cycle, no depth counter exists in any of them, and the nesting of tables/arrays in the attacker-supplied message therefore controls recursion depth, exhausting the stack (StackOverflowError). What it says is exploitable is the unbounded mutual recursion itself, not something adjacent.
